faq.a: EUS provides >1 mm resolution and layer detail, allowing precise localisation and safe FNA, which CT cannot achieve.
faq.q: Why is EUS better than CT for small submucosal lesions?

faq.a: EUS can visualise and sample strictures, but therapeutic drainage still requires ERCP or percutaneous access.
faq.q: Can EUS replace ERCP for biliary obstruction?

faq.q: What if EUS is not available in my hospital?

exam: A 58‑year‑old man with painless jaundice and a 2.5 cm pancreatic head mass on ultrasound – what is the next step and why? — EUS‑FNA to obtain tissue before deciding on surgery or palliative stenting.

During EUS you see a 1 cm hypoechoic gastric wall lesion arising from layer 4 – how do you differentiate GIST from leiomyoma? — Perform EUS‑guided FNA; immunohistochemistry (c‑KIT, DOG1) confirms GIST, guiding tyrosine‑kinase inhibitor therapy.

A patient with HIV presents with mediastinal lymphadenopathy on chest X‑ray; EUS shows multiple hypoechoic nodes. What are the main differential diagnoses and how would you confirm? — TB lymphadenitis vs lymphoma vs metastatic cancer; obtain FNA for acid‑fast stain, culture, and cytology.

You are in a district hospital without EUS and suspect a pancreatic cyst. How do you manage? — Use abdominal ultrasound to assess size; if >6 cm, symptomatic, or infected, arrange referral for drainage or surgery; otherwise monitor with serial scans.

After EUS‑guided FNA of a pancreatic mass, the patient develops severe abdominal pain and fever. What is your immediate management? — Recognise possible pancreatitis or infection; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and arrange urgent imaging.
Explain why EUS is contraindicated in patients with severe coagulopathy. — Needle puncture can cause uncontrolled bleeding; correct coagulation parameters before the procedure.

A 45‑year‑old woman with chronic pancreatitis has a 3 cm pseudocyst causing early satiety. How does EUS guide treatment? — EUS can visualise cyst wall and vessels, allowing safe transgastric drainage with a stent, avoiding surgery.
What are the limitations of EUS in staging gastric cancer? — Cannot reliably assess distant metastases; requires CT or laparoscopy for M staging.
ai.title: Endoscopic Ultrasound
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) combines endoscopy and high‑frequency ultrasound to visualise the gastrointestinal wall and adjacent structures. It is essential for staging GI cancers, sampling lesions, and guiding therapy, especially where cross‑sectional imaging is limited.

b: Provides layer‑by‑layer view of GI wall
Allows fine‑needle aspiration (FNA) of deep lesions
Higher resolution than CT for small (<1 cm) lesions
sections.p: EUS uses a flexible endoscope with an ultrasound transducer at its tip. The probe emits 5‑20 MHz sound waves that create real‑time images of the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, and serosa, plus nearby organs such as pancreas, bile ducts, and mediastinum.

t.b: What is the depth and layer of a lesion? – Determines if a tumour is mucosal, submucosal, or beyond the muscularis, guiding management.
Is the lesion malignant? – Cytology/histology confirms cancer, lymphoma, or granuloma; if unavailable, rely on imaging and clinical context.

sections.p: The GI wall is visualised as five layers on EUS; recognising which layer a lesion arises from narrows the differential. In low‑resource settings, EUS often substitutes for CT or MRI in staging pancreatic and biliary cancers.

t.b: How to stage cancer without EUS? – Use ultrasound abdomen, plain radiographs, and clinical staging (e.g., weight loss, jaundice).

b: Evaluating biliary strictures when ERCP fails
Guiding drainage of cystic lesions in resource‑limited settings
sections.p: EUS is most valuable for pancreatic head masses, subepithelial gastric lesions, and mediastinal lymph nodes. In East African hospitals, it helps differentiate TB lymphadenitis from malignant nodes and guides drainage of pancreatic pseudocysts when surgery is not feasible.

t.b: Can the cyst be safely drained? – If cyst >6 cm, symptomatic, or infected, drainage reduces sepsis risk; otherwise observe.

b: Know the TNM criteria for pancreatic cancer on EUS (e.g., tumour >2 cm invading beyond muscularis = T3).
Identify when to request EUS‑FNA versus when to proceed to surgery based on lesion size and patient fitness.
Explain why EUS is preferred over CT for small (<1 cm) lesions.
sections.p: Examiners test integration of anatomy, staging criteria, and decision‑making when EUS is unavailable.

b: Assuming all hypoechoic lymph nodes are cancer – consider TB, HIV‑related lymphoma.
Neglecting to assess vascular involvement – crucial for resectability.
Failing to arrange histology when imaging is equivocal.
sections.p: Pitfalls include over‑reliance on a single EUS view, misinterpreting inflammatory nodes as malignant, and forgetting alternative diagnoses common in the tropics.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging pancreatic mass with obstructive jaundice
Severe abdominal pain with peritonitis after EUS‑guided drainage
Uncontrolled bleeding from a puncture site
